title: Types of Sentences and Sentence Structure

steps.settingDescription: Hundreds of royal petitions pile up on four sorting trays while Chikoo frantically stamps every envelope with the wrong seal.

dialogues.line: Chikoo! Why did you stamp 'Where is the missing fountain pen?' as an ORDER? And why did you stamp 'What a brilliant goal!' as a QUESTION?
They all looked like sentences to me, Your Majesty! I did not know sentences have moods AND secret clause skeletons!
Sentences are sorted two ways: by PURPOSE (Declarative, Interrogative, Imperative, Exclamatory) and by CLAUSE STRUCTURE (Simple, Compound, Complex).
Master both sorting tables, and you can build crisp reports or rich multi-clause arguments whenever you want!

steps.storyCallout: Goal: Classify sentences by communicative purpose AND by Simple, Compound, and Complex clause structure.

steps.subtopicTitle: Kinds of Sentences by Communicative Function
steps.memoryAidLabel: Memory Aid (Peculiar Definition — Not a Formal Rule)
steps.peculiarDefinition: Sentences wear four hats: the Reporter (Statement), the Detective (Question), the Coach (Command/Request), and the Cheerleader (Exclamation).
steps.formalDefinition: By communicative function, sentences are classified into four kinds: Declarative (assertive statements), Interrogative (questions), Imperative (commands, requests, or advice), and Exclamatory (strong sudden feelings).
steps.simpleExplanation: Look at both the speaker's intention and the grammatical pattern: Declaratives state facts or opinions and end with '.'; Interrogatives invert auxiliary and subject and end with '?'; Imperatives start with a base verb (or 'Please / Don't') with implied subject 'you'; Exclamatives often open with 'What a...' or 'How...' and end with '!'.

structurePatterns.sample: Our school won the inter-district quiz. / The library is not open on Sundays.
Did you bring the geometry box? / Why is the bus delayed?
Turn left at the clock tower. / Please pass the salt.

structurePatterns.formula: What (a/an) + Noun Phrase / How + Adj/Adv + Subject + Verb!
structurePatterns.sample: How swiftly the goalkeeper dived! / What a peaceful morning it is!

realLifeExamples.sentence: Check your spelling before submitting the form.
What an inspiring speech Dr. Bose delivered!
realLifeExamples.contextNote: Exclamatory starting with 'What an...' + noun phrase.

correctVsIncorrect.whyItHappens: In an exclamatory sentence beginning with 'How...' or 'What...', keep normal Subject + Verb order ('the sunset is') rather than question inversion ('is the sunset').

exceptions: Polite requests dressed as questions ('Could you close the window?') use interrogative grammar to perform a polite request.

steps.storyPrompt: Maharaj Vakya holds up an urgent scroll: "Do not feed bananas to the royal pigeons!"
steps.questionPrompt: Which kind of sentence is this?
options: Declarative (Assertive)
Interrogative
Imperative
Exclamatory
steps.hint: Look at the opening ('Do not feed...')—is it asking a question, stating a fact, or giving an instruction/prohibition?
steps.feedbackCorrect: Maharaj Vakya: "Correct! Negative commands starting with 'Do not + base verb' are Imperative sentences—even when they end with an exclamation mark!"
steps.feedbackWrongDefault: Look past the exclamation mark at the grammar: 'Do not feed...' gives a direct command to an understood 'you'.

feedbackWrongByOption.Exclamatory: Careful! Punctuation alone doesn't make it Exclamatory—commands spoken forcefully can take '!', yet remain Imperative.

steps.simplerExample: Please stay quiet. / Don't touch the wet paint. (Both are Imperatives).

steps.stepTitle: Discover: Simple, Compound and Complex Sentences
steps.subtopicTitle: Simple, Compound and Complex Sentence Structures
steps.memoryAidLabel: Memory Aid (Peculiar Definition — Not a Formal Rule)
steps.peculiarDefinition: A Simple sentence is a solo bicycle (1 main clause). A Compound sentence is a tandem bike where two equal riders pedal side by side (linked by FANBOYS). A Complex sentence is a scooter towing a sidecar (1 main clause + 1 or more dependent subordinate clauses).
steps.formalDefinition: By clause structure: a Simple sentence has exactly one independent (main) clause; a Compound sentence joins two or more independent clauses of equal rank using coordinating conjunctions (and, but, or, nor, for, yet, so); a Complex sentence contains one main clause and at least one subordinate (dependent) clause introduced by a subordinator or relative word.
steps.simpleExplanation: Count the FINITE verbs to count the clauses! A Simple sentence has just ONE finite verb (though it may have compound subjects or non-finite phrases like 'to win'). Compound sentences link independent halves that can stand alone. Complex sentences join a main clause with a dependent clause ('because...', 'when...', 'although...', 'who...').

structurePatterns.formName: Simple Sentence (1 Main Clause, 1 Finite Verb)
structurePatterns.sample: In spite of the heavy rain, the match continued.

structurePatterns.formula: Main Clause + Coordinating Conjunction (for, and, nor, but, or, yet, so) + Main Clause
structurePatterns.sample: It rained heavily, yet the match continued.

structurePatterns.formula: Main Clause + Subordinating Conjunction / Relative + Subordinate Clause
structurePatterns.sample: Although it rained heavily, the match continued.

realLifeExamples.sentence: Hearing the bell, the students hurried to class.
realLifeExamples.contextNote: Simple sentence! 'Hearing' is a non-finite participle; 'hurried' is the ONLY finite verb.

realLifeExamples.sentence: The bell rang, and the students hurried to class.
realLifeExamples.contextNote: Compound sentence: two equal main clauses joined by 'and'.

realLifeExamples.sentence: When the bell rang, the students hurried to class.
realLifeExamples.contextNote: Complex sentence: dependent time clause ('When the bell rang') + main clause.

correctVsIncorrect.incorrectSentence: Although I studied hard, but I found the puzzle tricky.
correctVsIncorrect.correctSentence: Although I studied hard, I found the puzzle tricky.
correctVsIncorrect.whyItHappens: Never combine a subordinator ('Although') AND a coordinator ('but') in the same two-clause sentence—pick one structure (Complex with 'Although' OR Compound with 'but').

exceptions: A Compound-Complex sentence combines at least two independent clauses and at least one dependent clause ('When the bell rang, Aarav packed his bag, and Meera locked the lab').

steps.storyPrompt: Vaani tests your eye on a tricky sentence: "Walking through the spice market, Ananya bought fresh turmeric."
steps.questionPrompt: What is the structure of Vaani's sentence?
options: Simple sentence
Compound sentence
Complex sentence
Compound-Complex sentence
steps.hint: Count the finite verbs! Is 'Walking' a finite verb with a subject, or a non-finite participial phrase?
steps.feedbackCorrect: Vaani: "Sharp eyes! 'Walking through the spice market' is a participial phrase—there is only ONE finite verb ('bought'), so it is a Simple sentence."
steps.feedbackWrongDefault: Count the finite verbs: only 'bought' is finite. No coordinating or subordinating clause connector appears.

feedbackWrongByOption.Complex sentence: Watch out for the trap! 'Walking...' is a phrase (no subject + finite verb), not a subordinate clause.

steps.simplerExample: Despite feeling tired (phrase), Kiran finished her drawing (1 finite verb = Simple).

steps.storyPrompt: Chikoo submits a complaint: "Because the bridge was slippery, therefore we took the longer road."
steps.questionPrompt: Choose the grammatically clean Complex (or Compound) correction:
options: Because the bridge was slippery, so we took the longer road.
Because the bridge was slippery, we took the longer road.
Although the bridge was slippery, therefore we took the longer road.
Because the bridge was slippery; and we took the longer road.
acceptedAnswers: Because the bridge was slippery, we took the longer road.
steps.hint: English does NOT use 'because ... so' or 'because ... therefore' together. Keep only one connector!
steps.feedbackCorrect: Acharya Vidyadhar: "Cleanly fixed! One subordinator ('Because') is all a Complex sentence needs."
steps.feedbackWrongDefault: Remove the extra 'so / therefore / and' when 'Because' already introduces the reason clause.
steps.simplerExample: Because it was late, we went home. (OR: It was late, so we went home.)

steps.storyPrompt: Assemble the mailroom label to explain why the celebration continued indoors.
steps.questionPrompt: Tap the tiles in order to form a well-punctuated Complex sentence:
acceptedAnswers: since the sky darkened, we shifted the games into the hall.
steps.hint: Notice the comma at the end of 'since the sky darkened,'—that subordinate clause comes first!
steps.feedbackCorrect: Acharya Vidyadhar: "Spot on! Subordinate clause first, comma, then the main clause."
steps.feedbackWrongDefault: Place the dependent 'since' clause (which ends with a comma) before the main clause ('we shifted the games into the hall.').
steps.simplerExample: Since it grew dark, we lit the lanterns.

steps.settingDescription: Every petition is neatly sorted into Statements, Questions, Commands, and Exclamations—and tagged Simple, Compound, or Complex.

dialogues.line: Look how smooth the sorting desk looks now! Not a single 'Although... but...' collision left.
How clearly our citizens write! (Exclamatory, Simple!) Proceed to the Grammar Notebook and Final Assessment!

steps.storyCallout: Module 3 Story Complete! Review your Grammar Notebook or attempt the 15-question assessment.

summaryRules.heading: Four Kinds by Function
summaryRules.ruleSummary: Declarative (states facts/opinions), Interrogative (asks questions), Imperative (commands/requests with implied 'you'), Exclamatory (strong emotion, often 'What a...' / 'How...').
summaryRules.example: How bright the stars look tonight! (Exclamatory)

summaryRules.heading: Simple, Compound, Complex
summaryRules.ruleSummary: Simple = 1 independent clause (1 finite verb); Compound = 2+ independent clauses joined by FANBOYS or ';'; Complex = 1 main clause + 1+ subordinate clauses.
summaryRules.formulaOrPattern: Simple (1 MC) | Compound (MC + coord + MC) | Complex (MC + sub + SC)
summaryRules.example: Simple: Working hard, Ira won. | Compound: Ira worked hard, and she won. | Complex: Because Ira worked hard, she won.

memoryAids: Four hats: Reporter (.), Detective (?), Coach (Command), Cheerleader (!).
Three rides: Solo bike (Simple), Tandem bike (Compound — FANBOYS), Scooter + Sidecar (Complex).

commonMistakes.incorrectSentence: Although he ran fast, yet he missed the bus.
commonMistakes.correctSentence: Although he ran fast, he missed the bus.
commonMistakes.whyItHappens: Do not use both 'although/though' and 'but/yet' together.
Exclamatory sentences keep Subject + Verb order instead of question inversion.

exceptions: Forceful imperatives ('Stop right there!') may end with '!' while remaining grammatically Imperative, not Exclamatory.
textbookNotes: Covers Kinds of Sentences and Simple, Compound, and Complex analysis across Classes IX–X.

questions.questionText: Classify: "Please keep your library books dry during the monsoon."
options: Declarative
Interrogative
Imperative
Exclamatory
questions.explanation: A polite request starting with 'Please + base verb' (with understood subject 'you') is an Imperative sentence.
questions.grammarRule: Requests, instructions, and commands are Imperative sentences.

questions.questionText: Which is the grammatically standard Exclamatory sentence?
options: How fast did the cheetah run!
How fast the cheetah ran!
What fast the cheetah ran!
Did the cheetah run how fast!
questions.explanation: 'How + adverb/adjective + Subject + Verb!' keeps declarative word order without 'did'-inversion.
distractorRationales: 'What' modifies noun phrases ('What a fast cheetah!'), not bare adverbs.
questions.grammarRule: Exclamatives with 'How' and 'What' keep Subject-before-Verb order.

questions.questionText: Which sentence is a SIMPLE sentence?
options: I opened the window, and a cool breeze blew in.
When I opened the window, a cool breeze blew in.
Opening the window, I felt a cool breeze.
I opened the window because the room was warm.
questions.explanation: 'Opening the window' is a non-finite participial phrase; 'felt' is the single finite verb, making it a Simple sentence.
questions.grammarRule: A Simple sentence contains exactly one finite clause.

options: Though it was foggy, the flight landed safely.
It was foggy, yet the flight landed safely.
Despite the fog, the flight landed safely.
Landing safely in the fog, the pilot smiled.
questions.explanation: Coordinating conjunction 'yet' joins two equal independent clauses: 'It was foggy' and 'the flight landed safely'.
distractorRationales: Correct: two independent clauses joined by 'yet'.
Simple ('Despite the fog' is a prepositional phrase).
questions.grammarRule: Compound sentences join independent clauses with coordinators (FANBOYS).

questions.questionText: Which of the following is a COMPLEX sentence?
options: Sunil and Kabir went to the book fair together.
Sunil bought a dictionary, and Kabir bought an atlas.
Sunil bought a dictionary that contains clear usage notes.
Sunil went to the book fair to buy a dictionary.
questions.explanation: 'that contains clear usage notes' is a dependent relative clause modifying 'dictionary', making the sentence Complex.
distractorRationales: Simple sentence with a compound subject.
Correct: main clause + subordinate relative clause.
Simple sentence ('to buy a dictionary' is an infinitive phrase).
questions.grammarRule: A main clause + a relative or adverb/noun subordinate clause forms a Complex sentence.

options: Because he practised daily, therefore he mastered the tabla.
Since he practised daily, so he mastered the tabla.
He practised daily, so he mastered the tabla.
As he practised daily, hence he mastered the tabla.
questions.explanation: Use either a subordinator alone ('Since he practised daily, he mastered...') OR a coordinator alone ('..., so he mastered...'), never both.
questions.grammarRule: Do not pair 'because/since/as' with 'so/therefore/hence' for the same two clauses.

questions.questionText: In "Before the curtains rose, the stagehands checked every microphone", which is the MAIN clause?
options: Before the curtains rose
the stagehands checked every microphone
checked every microphone
Before the curtains
questions.explanation: 'the stagehands checked every microphone' can stand independently as a complete sentence, whereas 'Before the curtains rose' depends on it.
questions.grammarRule: The main clause expresses the independent core proposition.

questions.questionText: Why is "Look out for that falling branch!" classified as Imperative rather than Exclamatory?
options: It ends with a question mark.
Its verb is in base imperative form directed at understood 'you' to warn/command.
It begins with 'What' or 'How'.
It has two subordinate clauses.
questions.explanation: Sentence classification depends on grammatical structure and function—'Look out...' is a base-verb command/warning to 'you'.
distractorRationales: It does not begin with 'What' or 'How'.
questions.grammarRule: An exclamation mark on a command does not convert an Imperative into an Exclamatory sentence.

questions.questionText: Why is "Meera and Tarun cleaned the science lab" a SIMPLE sentence rather than Compound?
options: Because 'and' joins two nouns inside ONE subject, not two separate clauses with two finite verbs.
Because it has no object.
Because 'cleaned' is in the past tense.
Because it is a question.
questions.explanation: A Compound sentence needs at least two independent clauses (each with its own finite verb). Here there is only one finite verb: 'cleaned'.
distractorRationales: Correct: compound subject + single finite verb = Simple sentence.
Tense doesn't decide simple vs. compound.
questions.grammarRule: A compound subject or compound object inside one clause still makes a Simple sentence.

questions.questionText: Which COMPLEX sentence accurately matches the Simple sentence "On seeing the police, the pickpocket fled"?
options: The pickpocket saw the police and fled.
As soon as the pickpocket saw the police, he fled.
The pickpocket fled on seeing the police.
Seeing the police, the pickpocket fled.
questions.explanation: 'As soon as the pickpocket saw the police' is a subordinate finite time clause attached to 'he fled'.
distractorRationales: Correct: Complex sentence with 'As soon as'.
Still Simple ('on seeing' is a phrase).
Still Simple ('Seeing' is a participle phrase).
questions.grammarRule: Convert a participial/prepositional time phrase into a finite clause with 'when/as soon as' to form a Complex sentence.

questions.questionText: Identify the sentence that is COMPOUND-COMPLEX:
options: When the bell rang, the students left.
The bell rang, and the students left.
When the bell rang, the students packed their bags, and the teacher locked the door.
Packing their bags quickly, the students left the classroom.
questions.explanation: It contains 1 subordinate clause ('When the bell rang') and 2 independent clauses ('the students packed their bags' + 'the teacher locked the door').

questions.questionText: What kind of sentence is "None of the clues pointed to Detective Ira"?
options: Declarative (negative)
Interrogative
Imperative
Exclamatory
questions.explanation: Declarative (assertive) sentences include both affirmative and negative statements.
distractorRationales: Correct: negative statement is still Declarative.
questions.grammarRule: Both affirmative and negative statements are Declarative sentences.

questions.questionText: How many finite clauses are in "To reach the summit before noon, the trekkers started early and carried extra water"?
options: One (it is a Simple sentence with a compound verb)
Two (because 'To reach' is a clause)
Three
Zero
questions.explanation: 'To reach' is a non-finite infinitive phrase; 'started and carried' share one subject ('the trekkers') in a single finite predicate (or compound predicate in one Simple sentence).
distractorRationales: Correct: infinitive phrase does not add a clause.
questions.grammarRule: Non-finite infinitives and participles form phrases, not finite clauses.

questions.questionText: Turn "It is a very clever solution" into a natural Exclamatory sentence:
options: What a clever solution it is!
How a clever solution it is!
What clever solution is it!
Is it what a clever solution!
questions.explanation: Use 'What a/an + adjective + singular countable noun + Subject + Verb!' for noun-focused exclamations.
distractorRationales: Correct: 'What a clever solution it is!'
'How' does not take 'a + noun'; use 'How clever the solution is!'.
questions.grammarRule: Use 'What + (a/an) + Noun Phrase + S + V!' and 'How + Adj/Adv + S + V!'.

questions.questionText: Which fix repairs the comma splice in "The bell rang, the students cheered"?
options: The bell rang, and the students cheered.
The bell rang the students cheered.
The bell rang because, the students cheered.
The bell ringing, the students cheered.
questions.explanation: Two independent clauses cannot be joined by a comma alone; add a coordinating conjunction ('and'), a semicolon, or a subordinator.
distractorRationales: Correct: comma + coordinating conjunction 'and' forms a valid Compound sentence.
Wait—actually 'The bell ringing' is an absolute phrase, whereas 'and' directly repairs the Compound sentence cleanly.
questions.grammarRule: Join two independent clauses with ', + FANBOYS' or a semicolon—never a bare comma.
